analysis.one_liner: Requires corporations, unions, Super PACs, and nonprofits to name big donors behind election ads.
analysis.headline: The bill had 42 Senate cosponsors, all Democrats and Independents, but died in the Rules Committee without ever getting a vote or a hearing before the 2015-2016 Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The DISCLOSE Act would have required any corporation, labor union, nonprofit group, or Super PAC that spends more than $10,000 on campaign ads to file a report with the Federal Election Commission within 24 hours, naming any donor who gave $10,000 or more toward that spending. It also widened the definition of a political attack ad so more ads would count as campaign spending, and stretched the period before an election during which ads must be reported. The goal was to let voters see who is paying for the political ads they watch. It was referred to the Senate Rules Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters, who would learn the identities of major donors behind campaign ads — including 'dark money' groups that today can spend without naming contributors — and candidates and campaigns targeted by undisclosed spending.

how_it_helps.text: Corporations, labor unions, and tax-exempt nonprofits that spend more than $10,000 on campaign-related communications in an election cycle would have to file a disclosure statement under penalty of perjury within 24 hours of crossing that threshold, listing each disbursement over $1,000. [S3]
The bill requires covered organizations to report the name and address of any person who gave $10,000 or more toward campaign spending, whether through segregated accounts or general funds. [S3]
It extends disclosure to Super PAC accounts that accept donations in unlimited amounts, requiring those accounts to report their donors. [S3]

It redefines an 'independent expenditure' to include communications that a reasonable person could only read as advocating a candidate's election or defeat, and lengthens the window (from 30 days to January 1 through election day for House and Senate ads) during which ads must be reported as electioneering communications. [S2]
Reports would be due at most 24 hours after each disclosure date, rather than only on periodic schedule, so donors to last-minute attack ads would be public before the election. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Corporations, labor unions, Super PACs, and nonprofit groups that spend money on political ads would bear new reporting and compliance costs, and their major donors would lose anonymity.

drawbacks.text: Compliance burden: covered organizations must file statements within 24 hours of crossing thresholds, name donors, and obtain CEO certifications that spending was not coordinated, which imposes real administrative costs, particularly on smaller nonprofits and unions. [S3]

Donor exposure: naming donors of $10,000 or more to advocacy groups can expose contributors to harassment or retaliation, and critics argue this chills participation in political debate — the objection courts and critics have raised to broad donor disclosure.
The bill broadens the definition of advocacy so that 'issue' ads mentioning a candidate's fitness for office are treated as election spending, which sweeps more speech into regulation. [S2]
It also repeals the existing prohibition on political contributions by individuals age 17 or younger, a loosening unrelated to its disclosure purpose. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — voters knowing who pays for the ads designed to sway their votes — is substantial and goes to the public, while the costs fall on big spenders and donors in money, compliance, and anonymity. The strongest good-faith objection is that naming donors can chill participation or expose people to harassment, and the expanded definition of political ads may sweep in some issue advocacy. The under-17 contribution repeal is a small unrelated loosening. On balance the bill is a straightforward transparency measure, though its breadth would have required careful FEC rulemaking.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the DISCLOSE Act of 2015 in the Senate on January 21, 2015. [S1]
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Rules and Administration the same day; no further action was ever taken. [S5]
The bill accumulated 42 cosponsors — 40 Democrats and 2 Independents — but no Republican cosponsors. [S4]
The bill never received a committee markup, a hearing, a floor vote, or a roll call in the Senate or House before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017. [S1] [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Major campaign spenders and their donors — corporations, Super PACs, and tax-exempt 'dark money' groups — remain free to fund election ads without naming their backers. Voters gained nothing from the bill's death; they simply never got the disclosure it offered. The outcome also spared officeholders who benefit from anonymous spending from having to defend it on the record.

for.name: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it on the Senate floor.

for.name: Sens. Bernie Sanders and Angus King

against.name: Senate Rules and Administration Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a markup, hearing, or vote on it during the two-year Congress.

against.name: Sen. Roy Blunt
against.role: Chair, Senate Rules and Administration Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair, controlled the committee that never acted on the bill.

against.name: Sen. Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: As majority leader, never brought the bill to the Senate floor, and has long opposed mandatory donor disclosure as a burden on political speech.

sides.party_line_note: All 42 cosponsors were Democrats or allied Independents (40 of 44 Senate Democrats plus both Independents); not a single Senate Republican signed on, and the bill died in a committee chaired by a Republican.

industries.industry: Corporate political spenders and Super PAC donors
industries.note: The bill would have forced companies and Super PAC accounts accepting unlimited donations to name anyone giving $10,000 or more toward campaign ads, ending their ability to influence elections anonymously. That anonymity is what the public pays for in uninformed votes.

These groups currently run political ads without disclosing funders; the bill would classify them as covered organizations required to report major donors and spending. Their business model of undisclosed influence is precisely what the bill targets.

Unions would face the same disclosure duties and compliance costs as corporations for political spending, losing anonymity for major contributors, while gaining the same transparency rules being imposed on their corporate opponents.

Firms handling political ads would have to process faster reporting windows and would see more of the election cycle (starting January 1 of the election year) fall under reporting rules, but the demand for their services would continue regardless of disclosure.
